key_terms.meaning: L is recursive (decidable) when some Turing machine halts on every input and accepts exactly the strings of L.
L is RE when some Turing machine accepts exactly the strings of L and may loop forever on strings not in L.
A machine that halts on every input; also called a decider for its language.
A problem whose set of 'yes' instances is a recursive language, so one machine always answers correctly.
A problem for which no Turing machine halts on every input with the correct yes or no.
A ≤m B when a total computable f gives w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B; if B is decidable then A is decidable.
HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : machine M halts on input w}; it is RE but not recursive.
Cantor's trick: build an object that differs from every item of a list at one position, so the list is incomplete.
For any nontrivial property P of RE languages, {⟨M⟩ : L(M) has P} is undecidable.
A property of RE languages that is true for at least one RE language and false for at least one other.
Given pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ), decide if some sequence i₁…i_k gives xᵢ₁…xᵢ_k = yᵢ₁…yᵢ_k; undecidable.
PCP with the extra rule that the matching sequence must start with pair 1; MPCP reduces to PCP.
f : Σ* → Σ* is computable when some machine halts on every input w with f(w) on its tape.
Some machine halts with f(w) where f is defined and loops forever where f is undefined.
The largest number of steps a machine takes over all inputs of length n.
The largest number of tape cells a machine visits over all inputs of length n.
P = ∪ₖ DTIME(nᵏ), the languages decided by a deterministic machine in polynomial time.
Languages whose 'yes' strings have a short certificate that a polynomial-time verifier accepts.
L ∈ NP and every language in NP reduces to L in polynomial time.
Every language in NP reduces to L in polynomial time; L itself need not lie in NP.

takeaways: A language is recursive when a machine decides it with a guaranteed halt, and RE when a machine only has to accept its strings.
Every recursive language is RE, but HALT shows the reverse fails.
A problem is undecidable when no single machine can answer every instance, not when we have not found one yet.
Diagonalization proves the halting problem undecidable by making a machine disagree with every machine in a list.
Rice's theorem turns one halting-style proof into undecidability for every nontrivial property of accepted languages.
PCP packages the power of Turing machine computation into a domino-matching puzzle, which is why it is undecidable.
Computable functions always halt with an answer; partial computable functions may loop where the value is undefined.
Time and space complexity are worst-case counts of steps and cells as functions of input length n.
P ⊆ NP, and an NP-complete problem is the hardest kind inside NP: a polynomial algorithm for one solves all of NP.
bank_note: Long answers here are graded on clean definitions, an explicit reduction or diagonal argument, and the conclusion drawn from it, so write the machine construction and the contradiction step by step.

bank.q: Define recursive and recursively enumerable languages. Prove that every recursive language is recursively enumerable and give an example of an RE language that is not recursive.
outline: Recursive: some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly L
RE: some TM accepts exactly L and may loop on strings outside L
Construction: run the decider, accept if it accepts, reject if it rejects, so the same machine is an acceptor
HALT is RE (simulate M on w and accept when it halts) but not recursive
Closure comment: recursive languages are closed under complement, RE ones are not

bank.q: State the halting problem formally. Explain, using diagonalization, why no Turing machine decides it.
outline: HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
Assume a decider H for HALT
Build D that on input ⟨M⟩ runs H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and does the opposite
D(⟨D⟩) halts iff D(⟨D⟩) loops, a contradiction
Conclusion: H does not exist; HALT is undecidable

bank.q: State Rice's theorem and use it to show that the language {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*} is undecidable.
outline: Theorem statement: nontrivial property of RE languages gives an undecidable index set
Property 'L(M) = Σ*' holds for some RE languages and fails for others, so it is nontrivial
Quote the theorem, or sketch the reduction from HALT for full marks
Conclusion: no machine decides whether a given machine accepts every string

bank.q: Define Post's correspondence problem and its modified version. Explain why MPCP is reduced to PCP and not the other way round.
outline: Domino pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ) over a finite alphabet, repetitions allowed
A solution is a nonempty index sequence with equal top and bottom strings
MPCP adds the rule that pair 1 must come first
Direction of reduction: MPCP ≤m PCP, so undecidability of MPCP gives undecidability of PCP
Both are undecidable

bank.q: Define the time complexity and space complexity of a Turing machine. Why do we ignore constant factors and use worst-case counts?
outline: Time: maximum steps over inputs of length n, written t(n)
Space: maximum tape cells scanned, written s(n)
Both are functions of the input length, not the input value
Worst case because an algorithm must work on every input
Constant factors and lower-order terms dropped since they do not change polynomial versus exponential

bank.q: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on the empty tape}. Show that L is undecidable by reducing the halting problem to it.
outline: Define a total computable map from ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩
M′ erases its tape, writes w, then simulates M
M halts on w iff M′ halts on empty tape
If L were decidable, HALT would be decidable, contradiction
Reduction works in one direction only; state it clearly

bank.q: Given domino pairs, find a matching sequence for a small PCP instance, and explain how a machine would generate candidate sequences.
outline: List the pairs with top and bottom strings
Try increasing sequence lengths, tracking the top and bottom partial strings
Stop when both strings are equal and nonempty
A machine can enumerate sequences in length order, so the problem is semidecidable
Why enumeration alone cannot decide the problem

bank.q: Show using Rice's theorem that the set of machine codes whose language is finite is undecidable.
outline: Property 'L(M) is finite' is a property of the language, not the machine
It is nontrivial: some RE languages are finite, some are infinite
Rice's theorem applies directly
Write the index set A = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) finite} and conclude it is undecidable
Note finiteness of the machine description is decidable, finiteness of the language is not

bank.q: Define a computable function and a partial computable function. Describe a Turing machine that computes f(n) = n² for unary n written as 1ⁿ, and state whether it is total.
outline: Computable: halts on every input with the correct output
Partial computable: halts and gives the value only where the value exists
Machine outline: count the 1s, write the product as repeated blocks of 1s
The machine halts on all unary inputs, so f is computable, hence total
Contrast with a function undefined on some inputs, which stays partial computable

bank.q: Show that if any NP-complete language lies in P, then P = NP.
outline: Definition: L is NP-complete if L ∈ NP and every A ∈ NP has A ≤p L
Polynomial reduction composes: A decided in polynomial time by deciding L
So if L ∈ P, every A ∈ NP is in P
Hence NP ⊆ P and, with P ⊆ NP, equality follows
Consequence for a practical problem such as SAT or 3-SAT

bank.q: Compare the diagonalization proof of the halting problem with a reduction proof of undecidability. When is each method the better tool?
outline: Diagonalization uses a self-reference trick and a hypothetical decider
Reduction assumes a decider for the new problem and builds one for a known undecidable problem
Reduction is reusable and gives relative hardness; diagonalization gives the first undecidable problem
Closure consequences: RE not closed under complement, recursive closed under complement
Rice's theorem as a mass-produced reduction

bank.q: Describe how Post's correspondence problem is used to prove that deciding ambiguity of a context-free grammar is undecidable.
outline: Build a grammar from the domino pairs so that top strings are generated by one side, bottom by the other
A matching sequence exists exactly when the grammar is ambiguous
So PCP ≤m ambiguity of CFG
Since PCP is undecidable, ambiguity is undecidable
Note many CFG problems are decidable (emptiness, membership) while ambiguity is not

bank.q: Explain what the Cook–Levin theorem says about SAT, and evaluate why the P versus NP question matters outside computer science.
outline: Cook–Levin: SAT is NP-complete
Certificate idea: a satisfying assignment is checked in polynomial time
Every NP problem reduces to SAT by writing the machine's computation as a Boolean formula
If P = NP, all NP problems become tractable; if not, none of the NP-complete ones are
Size of the search space, 2ⁿ certificates, and consequences for scheduling, routing, verification

bank.q: Prove that a language L is recursive if and only if both L and its complement are recursively enumerable.
outline: Forward: a decider for L also decides its complement, both are RE
Backward: run the two acceptors for L and its complement in parallel on the same input
Exactly one of them must eventually accept, so the parallel machine halts
This makes L recursive and its complement recursive too
Consequence: an RE language whose complement is not RE cannot be recursive; HALT is the standard example

glossary.def: An abstract machine with a finite state control, one tape and a read-write head that moves one cell per step.
A machine that takes a code for any machine M and an input w and simulates M on w.
The claim that every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine.
A Turing machine that halts on every input, so it always gives an answer.
A language accepted by some decider.
A language accepted by some Turing machine, which may loop on strings outside the language.
The class of languages whose complement is recursively enumerable.
A total computable mapping that turns instances of one problem into instances of another while preserving yes and no answers.
The problem of deciding, for a machine M and input w, whether M halts on w.
A proof method that builds an object differing from every member of a listed family at one selected point.
Every nontrivial property of the language accepted by a Turing machine is undecidable.
A condition that depends only on the set L(M), not on how the machine is written.
An ordered pair of strings (xᵢ, yᵢ) in an instance of Post's correspondence problem.
Post's correspondence problem with the added requirement that the first pair used is pair 1.
A function for which some Turing machine halts on every input with the correct output.
A function computed by a machine that halts with the right value where the function is defined and may loop elsewhere.
A worst-case count of machine steps as a function of input length.
A worst-case count of tape cells used as a function of input length.
The class of languages decided by a deterministic Turing machine in time O(t(n)).
Languages decidable by a deterministic machine in time bounded by a polynomial in the input length.
Languages for which a polynomial-time verifier accepts some short certificate exactly for the strings in the language.
A short string that lets a verifier confirm membership, such as a satisfying assignment for a formula.
A deterministic polynomial-time machine that reads the input and a certificate and accepts or rejects.
A language in NP to which every language in NP reduces in polynomial time.
A language to which every language in NP reduces in polynomial time, with no requirement of membership in NP.
A reduction computed by a deterministic machine in time polynomial in the input length, written A ≤p B.
